issues.legal_issue: A state government’s ownership of land and minerals does not make its proposal to reserve the area for a state-owned undertaking binding on the central government.
material_facts: The state government proposed that land be reserved for exploitation by a state-owned company.
The proposed land was not held under a prospecting licence or mining lease, but the central government did not approve the proposal.
issues.conclusion: The state government may propose reservation of eligible land for a state-owned undertaking, but reservation requires the central government’s approval.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 17A(2) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, the state government may propose reservation of land not held under a prospecting licence or mining lease for operations through a state-owned or controlled government company or corporation, but only with central government approval. The Act places regulation of mines and mineral development within the Union’s domain under Section 2. Indian Metals and Ferro Alloys Ltd. v. Union of India, Indian Charge Chrome Ltd. v. Union of India, State of T.N. v. M.P.P. Kavery Chetty, and State of Kerala v. Kerala Rare Earth & Minerals Ltd. support the requirement of central approval.

predicates.state_government_seeks_reservation_for_s: A state government asks that an area be reserved for prospecting or mining through a government company or corporation owned or controlled by it.
predicates.proposed_area_not_held_under_prospecting: The proposed area is not held under a prospecting licence or mining lease.

issues.definition: When a state government seeks to reserve an area not held under a prospecting licence or mining lease for its own government operator, central government approval is required for the reservation.

issues.legal_issue: The central government must independently assess a state reservation request and may consider all relevant factors, including government policy, economic considerations, public interest, and security.
material_facts: The central government reviewed a state government request to reserve land for a state-owned company.

The central government considered that private applicants had completed reconnaissance and applied for prospecting licences, as well as the national mineral policy’s support for private investment and the absence of a security or specific public-interest reason for reservation.
issues.conclusion: The central government may independently consider all factors relevant to whether reservation should be made, and is not confined to factors expressly stated in the Act or its rules.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17A(2) does not prescribe exclusive parameters for the central government’s decision. Under Section 2, regulation of mines and mineral development is within the Union’s domain. A relevant government policy may be considered; the National Mineral Policy, 2008, including its aim of a regulatory environment conducive to private investment, was relevant here. Sandur Manganese and Iron Ores Ltd. v. State of Karnataka supports the principle that government action in this field must be consistent with the statutory framework.

predicates.central_review_of_state_reservation_requ: The central government is considering a state government’s request to reserve an area for a state-owned operator.

issues.definition: When the central government reviews a state reservation request, it may independently consider all factors relevant to whether the area should be reserved.

issues.legal_issue: A reconnaissance permit and the preferential right associated with it do not themselves bar reservation under the state-reservation provision, although the reconnaissance and related applications may be considered as part of the central government’s assessment.
material_facts: The private applicants had reconnaissance permits, completed reconnaissance, and applied for prospecting licences.
The land was not held under a prospecting licence or mining lease when the state government sought reservation.
The central government considered the completed reconnaissance and pending prospecting applications among other relevant factors.
issues.conclusion: A reconnaissance permit does not prevent a reservation proposal under Section 17A(2), and the central government may consider the permit and its consequences among other factors but cannot reject the proposal solely because a reconnaissance permit was granted.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17A(2) bars reservation of land held under a prospecting licence or mining lease, but does not include a reconnaissance permit in that bar. Section 11(1) provides a preference to a reconnaissance-permit holder when an application for a prospecting licence is considered; that preference does not defeat a reservation proposal. Indian Charge Chrome Ltd. v. Union of India describes the reservation power as independent of the preference provisions. The reconnaissance-permit facts may nevertheless be considered with other relevant factors.

predicates.central_review_of_state_reservation_requ: The central government is considering a state government’s request to reserve an area for a state-owned operator.
predicates.land_is_covered_by_reconnaissance_permit: A reconnaissance permit covers the area, but no prospecting licence or mining lease holds it.

issues.definition: When the central government reviews a reservation request for land covered only by a reconnaissance permit, that permit does not itself bar reservation.

issues.legal_issue: A valid reservation requires the area to be unheld under a prospecting licence or mining lease, central government approval, and an official gazette notification specifying the area’s boundaries and the minerals reserved.
material_facts: The proposed area was not held under a prospecting licence or mining lease.
The central government had not approved the proposal, and the state government had not issued a gazette notification specifying the area’s boundaries or the minerals to be reserved.
issues.conclusion: Only the requirement that the land not be held under a prospecting licence or mining lease was met; there was no valid reservation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17A(2) requires that the area not be held under a prospecting licence or mining lease, that the central government approve the reservation, and that the state government notify the reservation in the Official Gazette while specifying the area’s boundaries and the mineral or minerals concerned. State of Kerala v. Kerala Rare Earth & Minerals Ltd. identifies these requirements for a valid reservation.

predicates.state_reservation_proposal: A state government proposes to reserve an area for operations through a state-owned or controlled government company or corporation.
predicates.area_not_held_under_prospecting_or_minin: The proposed area is not held under a prospecting licence or mining lease.
predicates.central_government_approval_obtained: The central government has approved the proposed reservation.
predicates.gazette_notification_specifies_boundarie: An official gazette notification specifies the boundaries of the area and the mineral or minerals to be reserved.

issues.definition: A state reservation is valid only when the area is unheld under a prospecting licence or mining lease, the central government has approved it, and the required gazette notification specifies its boundaries and minerals.

issues.legal_issue: The central government was justified in rejecting the reservation proposal after considering relevant factors, and the applicants’ prospecting-licence applications remained for consideration.
material_facts: The private applicants had completed reconnaissance under their permits, submitted reports, and applied for prospecting licences before the state government sought reservation.

The central government found that the reservation request was made at a belated stage, conflicted with the national mineral policy’s support for private investment, and was not supported by security considerations or a specific public-interest need.
The state government had not obtained central approval or issued a notification specifying the area’s boundaries and minerals.
The High Court quashed the central government’s rejection, and the matter came before the Supreme Court in appeals.
issues.conclusion: The central government’s rejection was justified. The High Court’s judgment was set aside, the rejection was upheld, and the state government was directed to consider the applicants’ prospecting-licence applications under the Act as amended in 2015.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 17A(2), the central government must independently decide whether to approve a reservation and may consider relevant policy and other factors, including private investment, economic considerations, public interest, and security. A reconnaissance permit does not bar reservation, but the central government cannot reject a proposal solely on that ground. Where no valid reservation has been made, the preference under Section 11(1) applies when the prospecting-licence applications are considered. The National Mineral Policy, 2008, was a relevant policy for the decision.

predicates.appeal_from_judgment_quashing_central_re: An appeal challenges a judgment that set aside the central government’s rejection of a state reservation request.
predicates.central_government_considered_relevant_f: The central government assessed relevant matters bearing on whether reservation should be approved, rather than relying solely on the existence of a reconnaissance permit.
predicates.applicants_completed_reconnaissance_and_: Private applicants completed reconnaissance and filed applications to move to the prospecting stage before the state sought reservation.
predicates.reservation_was_not_completed: The state had not obtained central approval and had not completed the required notification of the area and minerals.

issues.definition: In an appeal concerning a quashed rejection, the rejection is justified when the central government considered relevant factors, private applicants had completed reconnaissance and applied for prospecting licences, and the proposed reservation was not completed.
